effect_mechanism: In these upper-middle-income settings the evidence is about succession on land that has been cleared or degraded, and about what speeds it up. A meta-analysis of Brazilian restored biomes finds that restored areas, regardless of the restoration technique, show higher diversity metrics than degraded areas such as agricultural lands and pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_2]. Tree species richness rose as a function of time since disturbance across an Atlantic rainforest chronosequence [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_1], with a forest estimated to need 65 years, range 23 to 178, to reach a proportion of 80% animal-dispersed species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_2]. Assisted recruitment shortens the wait: beneath framework-species plantings in Thai dry forest, tree seedlings of many species recruited, 25 of them animal-dispersed and 11 wind-dispersed [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wydhayagarn09_1], and artificial perches produced native zoochoric regenerants that were absent from planted rings, so bringing in dispersers mattered more than the planting itself [ev_biodiversity_outcome_loureiro21_1]. On Turkmen barkhan sands the compiler records that the vegetation now provides the habitat for 25-27 species of plants and animals and rates habitat diversity as increased [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1529_2012_habitat_diversity]. Holding the cover is the companion mechanism: under community forest management in the Sierra Norte de Puebla, forest cover did not decline after the handover but increased by 8% [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1].
conditionality: The direction is consistent. Beyond the Brazilian meta-analysis the base is chronosequences and site studies, a compiler rating, and a forest-cover change read from land-use maps as a proxy for habitat rather than a count of species [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1]. In the same Brazilian meta-analysis, abundance in restored systems often did not differ from that in pastures and agricultural lands; the authors treat abundance as a poor indicator of recovery, so this null does not cut against the diversity gain [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_3]. Where a project was independently evaluated the result was less flattering — biodiversity is hard to assess, the management-effectiveness tool used was not a suitable proxy, and there was no clear-cut evidence that a Vietnamese special-use forest project improved biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ieg18_1]. Time is the binding condition: the Atlantic-forest estimate spans decades to well over a century before the assemblage approaches the composition of a mature forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_2], so nothing here promises a measurable result inside a project cycle. Read the gains with care. The gains are measured against the degraded or cleared starting point, not against intact forest, and a young stand holding less than old-growth is incomplete recovery rather than loss. And the perch and framework-species findings are about assisting dispersal into a restoration site [ev_biodiversity_outcome_loureiro21_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wydhayagarn09_1]: they presuppose a seed source within reach, which is a siting condition a scan can test and a restoration in a cleared landscape may fail.

effect_mechanism: Restoring forest on degraded land rebuilds habitat structure, and diversity follows. A global meta-analysis of 221 study landscapes found that forest restoration enhances biodiversity by 15 to 84% and vegetation structure by 36 to 77% compared with degraded ecosystems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles16_1]. A meta-analysis of Brazilian restored biomes finds that restored areas, regardless of the restoration technique, show higher diversity metrics than degraded areas such as agricultural lands and pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_2]. In Tigray, Ethiopia, the authors of an integrated landscape programme credit improved biodiversity to afforestation and area closures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2].
conditionality: The strong class rests on the meta-analyses, which compare restored sites with degraded land rather than with intact forest, and which do not separate the restoration route, so they cannot attribute the gain to a particular restoration family; in the global meta-analysis, restored sites are secondary or selectively logged forests [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles16_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_2]. In the same Brazilian meta-analysis, abundance in restored systems often did not differ from that in pastures and agricultural lands; the authors treat abundance as a poor indicator of recovery, so this null does not cut against the diversity gain [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_3]. The Tigray gain is a qualitative observation inside a bundle of afforestation, area closures and water-harvesting works, with no measured biodiversity metric [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2]. Only the Tigray unit comes from a low-income setting.

effect_mechanism: Natural regeneration rebuilds biodiversity as secondary forest develops. Across tropical chronosequences species richness recovers fastest and composition slowest, with richness after 20 years at 78% of old-growth values [ev_biodiversity_outcome_poorter21_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_poorter21_2]; tree species richness in Brazil's Atlantic Forest rises with time since disturbance [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_1]; and in the western Andes of Colombia restored bird and dung beetle communities closely resembled those of old growth forests after 15–30 yr [ev_biodiversity_outcome_chazdon16_1]. A pantropical meta-analysis finds natural regeneration outperforms active planting for plants, birds and invertebrates [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles17_1], and in Senegal's southern Groundnut Basin woody species richness in exclosures rose from 27 species after 1 year to 51 species after 5 and 12 years, an increase of more than 52% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1].
conditionality: Recovery of composition and endemism is slow: composition after 20 years was only 33% of old-growth values [ev_biodiversity_outcome_poorter21_1], and in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest regaining mature-forest endemism was estimated to take 1987 years [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_3]. The meta-analysis compares regeneration with planting rather than with degraded land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles17_1], and the Senegal result compares exclosures of different ages at one site rather than exclosures with open grazed land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1]. The gain accrues to the regenerating forest and the landscape, not to the adopting farmer's fields.

effect_mechanism: The units that set the class point toward a biodiversity loss, but none states how large it is. A review of nature-based solutions states that if non-native tree plantations replace intact native ecosystems such as ancient grasslands, peatlands or woodlands, the outcomes for biodiversity will be poor [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_1]. On the Orissa coast of India, extensive Casuarina plantations established as a storm protection measure caused destruction to olive ridley sea turtle nesting beaches [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badola05_12]. The same review reports research in north-west India showing that although afforestation activities can lead to an aggregate increase in forest cover, in most cases they result in loss of diversity and promote monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_4]. Against this, the review allows a gain in a narrower case: establishing plantations of non-native trees in a highly degraded landscape might benefit biodiversity locally if the trees enable native vegetation to regenerate, or regionally if plantations take pressure off native biodiverse forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_2]. An INRAE expert synthesis's own small meta-analysis of species richness in plantations against natural regeneration of the stand after regeneration cutting finds no clear difference: -0.24, a very imprecise estimate from a very small number of cases, with an interval that spans zero [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_1].
conditionality: The loss is stated without a size: the loss-side units are review statements and a cited case, none of which quantifies the decline against the land a plantation replaced, so the row reports a direction only and its strength is not quantified. What separates loss from gain is what the plantation replaces: intact native ecosystems, a nesting beach or a diverse cover replaced by monocultures on the loss side [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_badola05_12, ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_4], a highly degraded landscape where the trees help native vegetation return on the gain side [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_2]. The only quantified comparison against regeneration is non-significant [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_1]. Further INRAE statements point toward loss — plantations generally lead to decreases in biodiversity, or at least to changes in composition at the expense of native species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_6], and a cited 40% loss of local species richness in forest plantations relative to uncut control forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_2] — but they are held out of the class because their comparator is reference forest, not the starting point of a restoration project, so they describe a shortfall from a natural baseline rather than a restoration effect. The INRAE evidence is temperate and boreal, and only the Indian cases come from the low- and lower-middle-income target; the north-west India finding was re-homed to this family from active planting because it describes monoculture afforestation. The plantation family is parked out of the forest-restoration roll-up, because plantation monocultures may not count as a nature-based solution, and this row is published on its own: read it as evidence about plantations, not about restoration toward a natural baseline.

effect_mechanism: Protection and community forest management retain and expand forest habitat. GEF sustainable forest management projects show less deforestation than matched areas without projects [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_2], community forest management in Nepal reduced deforestation [ev_landscape_forest_cover_iufro20_1], and forest cover increased by 8% under community management in Mexico's Sierra Norte de Puebla [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1]. A global analysis of community forests found environmental condition improved after community forest management in 56% of the 524 cases tracking it [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1]. WOCAT compilers rate diversity as increased under protection: in India plant species diversity rose with improved moisture availability, soil conditions and microclimate, and the area provides more water and habitat for small animals and birds [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_animal_diversity]; in Afghanistan migratory animals and birds returned due to the protection measures and the prohibition of human activities [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_7460_2024_animal_diversity]. Forest governance instruments retain forest habitat: a meta-analysis of payments for environmental services found improved forest cover (SMD = 0.32, 95% CI [0.10, 0.55]) and reduced deforestation (SMD = −0.12) against comparison areas [ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_2]; in a systematic review of decentralised forest management, community-managed Van Panchayats in India improved the annual forest cover change rate by 0.40 percentage points and decentralised administration of protected forests in Bolivia by 0.80 percentage points [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_3]. World Bank evaluations report reduced deforestation, regeneration of degraded forests and protection of biodiversity under participatory forest management, and less deforestation under Bank-supported payment schemes in some countries [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_ieg13_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1], and in Bolivia most payment-like initiatives showed marked or intermediate environmental protection effects, and the rest weak ones [ev_biodiversity_outcome_robertson05_1].
conditionality: Most units measure forest cover, deforestation or threat reduction, a component proxy for biodiversity, and the Mexican figure is a before-after comparison with no counterfactual [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1]. In south-west Madagascar transfers of management to communities were found superficial and unable to stop forest clearing [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2], and GEF project sites likely exposed to urban encroachment showed forest losses [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_3]; the GEF evidence concerns existing forest under a bundle of protection and management rather than restoration. Governance effects are uneven: in the global community-forest analysis environmental condition decreased in 32% of community-forest cases [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1]; under Van Panchayats the change in broadleaf crown cover was insignificant (0.026 percentage points) [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_2], an evaluation of Vietnam's special-use forests found no clear-cut evidence that the project improved biodiversity, noting that its tracking tool was not a suitable proxy [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ieg18_1], and Bank-supported payment schemes were applied broadly rather than targeting high-value forest areas [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1]. These governance units measure forest cover, deforestation or threat reduction rather than species, the Indian and Bolivian estimates are cited in a systematic review, and the World Bank statements report outcomes only where they were monitored.

World Bank evaluations report reduced deforestation, regeneration of degraded forests and protection of biodiversity under participatory forest management, and less deforestation under Bank-supported payment schemes in some countries [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_ieg13_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1], and in Bolivia most payment-like initiatives showed marked or intermediate environmental protection effects, and the rest weak ones [ev_biodiversity_outcome_robertson05_1].
justification.conditionality: Most units measure forest cover, deforestation or threat reduction, a component proxy for biodiversity, and the Mexican figure is a before-after comparison with no counterfactual [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1]. In south-west Madagascar transfers of management to communities were found superficial and unable to stop forest clearing [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2], and GEF project sites likely exposed to urban encroachment showed forest losses [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_3]; the GEF evidence concerns existing forest under a bundle of protection and management rather than restoration. Governance effects are uneven: in the global community-forest analysis environmental condition decreased in 32% of community-forest cases [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1]; under Van Panchayats the change in broadleaf crown cover was insignificant (0.026 percentage points) [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_2], an evaluation of Vietnam's special-use forests found no clear-cut evidence that the project improved biodiversity, noting that its tracking tool was not a suitable proxy [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ieg18_1], and Bank-supported payment schemes were applied broadly rather than targeting high-value forest areas [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1]. These governance units measure forest cover, deforestation or threat reduction rather than species, the Indian and Bolivian estimates are cited in a systematic review, and the World Bank statements report outcomes only where they were monitored.

effect_mechanism: Across the restoration families taken together, carbon removals are real but uneven between families; they are stored in biomass as the trees grow and in soil organic carbon after the land-use transition. On biomass, natural regeneration removed 9.1 to 18.8 t CO2 per hectare per year during the first 20 years of growth [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_3]. Stock estimates line up with those rates: a 20-year-old secondary natural forest in the moist tropical biome was estimated at 51 t of aboveground carbon per hectare [ev_carbon_sequestration_busch19_1], the median present value of 30-year accumulation from natural regeneration is 60.2 tC per hectare in above- and belowground biomass and soil [ev_carbon_sequestration_busch24_1], and regeneration over 215 Mha could sequester 23.4 Gt of carbon in aboveground biomass over 30 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_williams24_1]. A meta-analysis of Brazilian restored biomes finds that restored areas, regardless of the restoration technique, hold more carbon than degraded agricultural lands and pastures [ev_carbon_sequestration_jakovac24_1]. Measured plantings show the accumulation directly: native-species restoration on former pasture held 21.85, 25.78 and 38.29 t C per hectare at three, five and seven years [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_3], and intervention sites were sequestering approximately 1.33 tons of carbon per hectare per year more than without the project [ev_carbon_sequestration_gefieo19_1]. On soils, across 151 transitions to forest the average carbon gain was 0.447% of pre-transition soil carbon per year [ev_soil_organic_carbon_busch19_1]; a meta-analysis of vegetation restoration in erosion zones found that returning cropland or bare land to forest raised soil organic carbon content by 25.28% compared with cropland [ev_soil_organic_carbon_yang23_3]; and a review of nature-based solutions adds that afforestation increases topsoil carbon in carbon-poor soils [ev_soil_organic_carbon_seddon21_5]. Practitioners give the same picture for biomass storage: the Niger compiler rates above-ground biomass as increasing, especially on pastoral and sylvo-pastoral land, the India compiler states that carbon storage is increased by the plantation, and the Honduras compiler that the change of agrarian land into forest reduces carbon and greenhouse gas emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_2325_2017_biomass_above_ground_C, ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_5243_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases, ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_750_2016_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. Avoided loss carries the rest: keeping existing cover through community management, payments and project support is counted here as retained carbon [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_iufro20_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_2], and environmental condition improved after community forest management in 56% of the 524 cases tracking it in a global analysis [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1].
conditionality: The class is slight because few of the units that point the same way say how big the removal is, and the biomass figures are growth rates over the first decades, not a permanent stock. A young restoration is also far from the reference it is growing towards — the same Atlantic-forest study that measured 21.85 to 38.29 t C per hectare in plantings aged three to seven years measured 138.94 in the mature forest [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_3] — which is incomplete recovery against intact forest, while the gain being claimed is against the pasture the planting replaced. Soil storage takes time to show: in the erosion-zone meta-analysis there was no significant increase in soil organic carbon under forestland compared with cropland in the first 0–5 years, and its gain is a change in carbon content rather than a stock [ev_soil_organic_carbon_yang23_5, ev_soil_organic_carbon_yang23_3]. The Brazilian meta-analysis reports carbon stocks against degraded references, not a net balance of removals [ev_carbon_sequestration_jakovac24_1]. Delivery is not guaranteed by the instrument: a REDD+ pilot in Nepal had an insignificant effect on total forest carbon [ev_carbon_sequestration_snilstveit19_1], management transfers in Madagascar did not halt clearing [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2], crown-cover gains in broadleaf forests under community management were insignificant [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_2], of 1,924 assessed project locations 33 showed strong evidence of harm and 169 no evidence of a benefit [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_3], and environmental condition decreased in 32% of community-forest cases [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1]. Planting can also lose carbon: the same review that reports topsoil gains in carbon-poor soils states that the associated soil disturbance causes significant losses in carbon-rich soils, especially of the deep soil carbon that takes many decades to accumulate [ev_soil_organic_carbon_seddon21_5], and that afforestation on peaty soils can lead to losses of soil carbon that outweigh that sequestered as the trees grow [ev_carbon_sequestration_seddon21_7]. Those are review sentences carrying cited findings, and they mark where planting reverses the sign: carbon-rich and peaty soils. Finally, weigh the mix: the largest totals are modelled potentials over large areas [ev_carbon_sequestration_williams24_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_busch24_1], the practitioner units are compiler ratings rather than measurements, and forest cover enters as a component proxy for carbon rather than as a stock measurement [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_1]. Plantation evidence is reported in its own row outside this roll-up and does not count here. The carbon removals are a landscape and climate benefit, accruing off-site rather than as a return on the farmer's own plot.

effect_mechanism: Secondary forest regrowing on cleared or abandoned land adds carbon removals through storage in biomass and soil. A global meta-analysis gives natural regeneration removal rates of 9.1–18.8 t CO2 per hectare per year during the first 20 years of forest regeneration [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_3]. Spatial models put the median 30-year carbon accumulation from natural regeneration at 60.2 tC per hectare in above- and below-ground biomass and soil [ev_carbon_sequestration_busch24_1], estimate 51 t of aboveground carbon per hectare in a 20-year-old secondary forest in the moist tropics [ev_carbon_sequestration_busch19_1], and estimate that regeneration over 215 Mha could sequester 23.4 Gt of C in aboveground biomass over a 30 year period [ev_carbon_sequestration_williams24_1]. Field chronosequences point the same way: Amazon secondary forests accumulated 50% (229 t/ha) of mature forest biomass after 25 years of first-cycle regrowth [ev_carbon_sequestration_gehring05_1], regenerating forests in the western Andes of Colombia reached about half of old-growth carbon stocks within 15–30 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_chazdon16_1], and an Atlantic Forest fragment regrown naturally for 60 years after complete clearing reached above-ground live biomass of 297 Mg/ha, close to the 313 Mg/ha of preserved forest nearby [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_5]. Soil carbon recovers fastest, reaching 90% of old-growth values in about 5 years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_poorter21_1], and across 151 transitions to forest the average soil carbon gain was 0.447% of pre-transition soil carbon per year [ev_soil_organic_carbon_busch19_1].
conditionality: Above-ground biomass recovers slowly: a pantropical analysis puts its recovery time at 12 decades, the slowest of the forest attributes measured [ev_carbon_sequestration_poorter21_1], so a project cycle captures only the early part of the storage gain. Much of the size evidence is modelled or pantropical, and the global potential holds only if the regrowing forests have the opportunity to establish and persist [ev_carbon_sequestration_williams24_1]. The field chronosequences are from upper-middle-income Brazil and Colombia, and the Amazon figure is biomass from slash-and-burn regrowth rather than carbon [ev_carbon_sequestration_gehring05_1]. Gains are measured against cleared or abandoned land; young regrowth holding less than old-growth is incomplete recovery, not a loss.

effect_mechanism: A global review finds planted forests and woodlots have the highest CO2 removal rates, 4.5 to 40.7 t CO2/ha/yr during the first 20 years of growth [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_1], and plantation reforestation with cyclical harvest accumulates a modelled median of 44.6 tC/ha across aboveground and belowground biomass, soil and harvested wood products [ev_carbon_sequestration_busch24_2]. Soil carbon also rises: afforestation of cropland raised soil organic carbon stocks by 26% on average and tropical transitions to plantation gained 0.919% of pre-transition soil carbon per year [ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_busch19_2], and the compiler for afforestation of degraded irrigated cropland in Uzbekistan reports surface biomass growth of 20 t/hectare/year and soil organic matter up by 20% in the form of fallen leaves [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1533_2011_biomass_above_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_1533_2011_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C]. A national-scale analysis for New Zealand puts the mean carbon growth rate of existing radiata pine forest at 8.5 tC per hectare, the rate it applies to new plantings on pasture [ev_carbon_sequestration_dymond12_3].
conditionality: Soil gains are conditional: on pastures (3%) and natural grasslands the change was not significantly different from zero, boreal sites lost 1.5% while other zones gained 7 to 17%, low-clay soils showed no change, heavily disturbed site preparation cut the gain to 4% against 19% with low disturbance, and plantation density made no difference [ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_4, ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_7, ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_9, ev_soil_organic_carbon_lagan09_10]; that meta-analysis draws mostly on high-income temperate sites. The New Zealand rate is a modelled growth rate for a production species that is nearly always harvested, so the stored carbon is given up at harvest, and it counts biomass uptake rather than a net greenhouse-gas balance [ev_carbon_sequestration_dymond12_3]. These are production-plantation results, planted forests, woodlots and plantations under cyclical harvest. Whether the plantation family belongs in the forest-restoration roll-up at all is an open decision for the team, so read this row as plantation evidence, not as restoration toward a natural baseline.

effect_mechanism: Protecting and managing forest keeps carbon stored in standing biomass and lets more build up. GEF sustainable forest management sites sequester more carbon each year than their counterfactual and avoid deforestation [ev_carbon_sequestration_gefieo19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_2], community forest management reduced deforestation in Nepal and increased forest cover in Puebla, Mexico [ev_landscape_forest_cover_iufro20_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1], environmental condition improved after community forest management in 56% of the 524 cases tracking it in a global analysis [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1], and the WOCAT compiler for community forests in Uttarakhand, India states that carbon storage is increased by the plantation, citing an average sequestration rate of 3.5 t ha -1 yr-1 for Van Panchayat forests [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_5243_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. Forest governance instruments keep carbon in standing forest by retaining cover: a meta-analysis of payments for environmental services found improved forest cover (SMD = 0.32, 95% CI [0.10, 0.55]) and reduced deforestation (SMD = −0.12) against comparison areas [ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_2]; community-managed Van Panchayats in India improved the annual forest cover change rate by 0.40 percentage points and decentralised administration of protected forests in Bolivia by 0.80 percentage points [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_3]; and World Bank evaluations report reduced deforestation and regeneration of degraded forests under participatory forest management, and a beneficial effect of payment schemes on deforestation in some countries [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_2, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1].
conditionality: The class is capped at moderate because few of the units pointing the same way say how big the effect is, and much of the evidence is forest-cover change used as a component proxy for carbon; the GEF carbon estimate is derived from a model over existing forest rather than measured stocks [ev_carbon_sequestration_gefieo19_1], and the India figure is a compiler's citation of earlier work rather than a measurement at the site [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_5243_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. Community management transfers in Madagascar did not halt clearing [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2], GEF sites under urban pressure showed harmful outcomes [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_3], environmental condition decreased in 32% of community-forest cases in the global analysis [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1], and the Mexican result has no counterfactual [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1]. justification.mechanism: Protecting and managing forest keeps carbon stored in standing biomass and lets more build up. GEF sustainable forest management sites sequester more carbon each year than their counterfactual and avoid deforestation [ev_carbon_sequestration_gefieo19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_2], community forest management reduced deforestation in Nepal and increased forest cover in Puebla, Mexico [ev_landscape_forest_cover_iufro20_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1], environmental condition improved after community forest management in 56% of the 524 cases tracking it in a global analysis [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1], and the WOCAT compiler for community forests in Uttarakhand, India states that carbon storage is increased by the plantation, citing an average sequestration rate of 3.5 t ha -1 yr-1 for Van Panchayat forests [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_5243_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. Forest governance instruments keep carbon in standing forest by retaining cover: a meta-analysis of payments for environmental services found improved forest cover (SMD = 0.32, 95% CI [0.10, 0.55]) and reduced deforestation (SMD = −0.12) against comparison areas [ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_2]; community-managed Van Panchayats in India improved the annual forest cover change rate by 0.40 percentage points and decentralised administration of protected forests in Bolivia by 0.80 percentage points [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_3]; and World Bank evaluations report reduced deforestation and regeneration of degraded forests under participatory forest management, and a beneficial effect of payment schemes on deforestation in some countries [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_2, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1].
justification.conditionality: The class is capped at moderate because few of the units pointing the same way say how big the effect is, and much of the evidence is forest-cover change used as a component proxy for carbon; the GEF carbon estimate is derived from a model over existing forest rather than measured stocks [ev_carbon_sequestration_gefieo19_1], and the India figure is a compiler's citation of earlier work rather than a measurement at the site [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_5243_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. Community management transfers in Madagascar did not halt clearing [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2], GEF sites under urban pressure showed harmful outcomes [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_3], environmental condition decreased in 32% of community-forest cases in the global analysis [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1], and the Mexican result has no counterfactual [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1]. Retention does not always show up as carbon: the REDD+ pilot in Nepal had an insignificant effect on total forest carbon in community forests (SMD = 0.09) [ev_carbon_sequestration_snilstveit19_1], the change in broadleaf crown cover under Van Panchayats was insignificant (0.026 percentage points) [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_2], and Bank-supported payment schemes were applied broadly rather than targeting high-value forest areas [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1]. The Nepal, Indian and Bolivian estimates are cited in systematic reviews, and the World Bank statements report outcomes only where they were monitored.

effect_mechanism: This row asks how much water leaves the catchment after forest cover is restored or expanded, and the evidence finds both less and more, with close to even weight on each side. Measured syntheses mostly find less: in about 80% of study cases reporting annual water yields the effect of forest restoration and other forms of forest cover expansion was a decrease, and in 6% an increase [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1]; baseflow decreased in 63% of cases [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_2]; groundwater levels or recharge decreased with forest cover expansion in 67% of the studies reporting them [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_filoso17_1]; and no study in the meta-analysis subset showed a water-yield gain [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3]. A global review found annual runoff fell significantly as forest cover rose in large watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_3]. The reason given is interception and use: tropical forest canopies commonly intercept up to 35 per cent of rainfall, and much of the water that soaks in is used by the trees [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1]. An FAO synthesis states that the effects of reforestation or afforestation on water yields are usually the reverse of those for forest removal, that low flows are usually diminished as well, especially where fast-growing, heavy water-using species are employed, and that planting forests on open land where the water table is close to the surface will lower groundwater levels [ev_water_yield_ham08_5, ev_water_yield_ham08_6, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_2]; after clearance, the streamflow gain declines as new cover establishes, and a return to pre-cut totals under natural regrowth may take more than eight years [ev_water_yield_ham08_8]. For planting, a global review warns that large-scale afforestation in water-limited environments will inevitably exacerbate water scarcity [ev_water_yield_zhang17_7]. On the gain side, baseflow from Ethiopian catchments with exclosures was 1.5 to 4 times greater than from cropland [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1]; a regional land-climate model projects significant increases of 11.4%, 16.9%, 17.6% and 84.9% in four regions under full reforestation potential [ev_water_regulation_teo22_1, ev_water_regulation_teo22_2, ev_water_regulation_teo22_3, ev_water_regulation_teo22_4]; about 19 small watersheds and a large watershed showed increased annual runoff due to forest cover gain, and spruce reforestation of a Heihe River headwater was predicted to increase annual runoff by 8.6% for a 12.6% increase in forest cover [ev_water_yield_zhang17_5, ev_water_yield_zhang17_6]; and forest succession and declining evapotranspiration may explain increased summer streamflow at two temperate forest sites logged in the early nineteenth century [ev_water_yield_jon12_3].
conditionality: What separates the sides is baseline, method, species and time. The losses come from measured syntheses that pool forest restoration with other forms of forest cover expansion [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1], from reviews of reforestation and afforestation, and from planting with fast-growing, heavy water-using species [ev_water_yield_ham08_6]. The gains are an exclosure-versus-cropland contrast rather than a comparison with unrestored land [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1], model projections at regional scale that work through precipitation as well as evapotranspiration [ev_water_regulation_teo22_1, ev_water_yield_zhang17_6], a minority of watersheds in a global review [ev_water_yield_zhang17_5], and a tentative attribution at sites logged in the early nineteenth century [ev_water_yield_jon12_3]. Some regions in the same model show nonsignificant declines where heightened evapotranspiration outstrips increases in precipitation [ev_water_regulation_teo22_5]. Several units are nulls: the global review failed to detect a statistically significant relationship between forest cover gain and annual runoff in small watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_2], and an FAO–CIFOR review states that interception should put to rest the belief that extensive reforestation or afforestation will increase low flows in the dry season [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1]. Scale matters within the losses too: the decrease shrinks at larger temporal and spatial scales in the systematic review [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3], while the global review finds the runoff reduction significant only in large watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_3]. The lowered water table under new forest is also described as improving drainage, so on waterlogged open land it is not purely a loss [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_2]. The review report that China's Grain-for-Green programme, planted mainly with fast-growing non-native species, reduced water supply has been re-homed to the plantation family, which is parked out of this roll-up; without that loss inside the restoration families the pool no longer leans towards less water, so no direction is stated. This row is for downstream users and basin planners: a loss here can coexist with local supply gains reported in the forest restoration water stress row, so read the two side by side rather than netting one against the other. Plantation results are reported in their own family row and do not count here.

An FAO synthesis states that the effects of reforestation or afforestation on water yields are usually the reverse of those for forest removal, that low flows are usually diminished as well, especially where fast-growing, heavy water-using species are employed, and that water yield after maturation remains below previous values where grassland is reforested with Pinus or Eucalyptus [ev_water_yield_ham08_5, ev_water_yield_ham08_6, ev_water_yield_ham08_9]; planting forests on open land where the water table is close to the surface will lower groundwater levels [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_2]. The gain side is modelling: under full reforestation potential, water yield increased in 7 of 15 Asia-Pacific regions, significantly in four, by 11.4%, 16.9%, 17.6% and 84.9% [ev_water_regulation_teo22_1, ev_water_regulation_teo22_2, ev_water_regulation_teo22_3, ev_water_regulation_teo22_4], and spruce reforestation of a Heihe River headwater was predicted to increase annual runoff by 8.6% [ev_water_yield_zhang17_6].
justification.conditionality: What separates the sides is method and species. The losses are review statements about reforestation and afforestation in general and about programmes using fast-growing or heavy water-using species; the gains are model projections for large regional reforestation scenarios rather than project-scale planting, and the same model shows nonsignificant declines in other regions where heightened evapotranspiration outstrips increases in precipitation [ev_water_regulation_teo22_5]. effect_mechanism: A global systematic review pooling forest restoration with forestry and afforestation found that annual water yield decreased in about 80% of study cases reporting it and increased in 6% [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1], baseflow decreased in 63% of cases [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_2], groundwater levels or recharge decreased in 67% of the studies reporting them [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_filoso17_1], and no water-yield gains were observed in the meta-analysed subset [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3]. A global review of forest change found a significant negative relationship between forest cover gain and annual runoff in large watersheds, so the reduction is only significant there [ev_water_yield_zhang17_3]. Tropical forest canopies commonly intercept up to 35 per cent of rainfall, which evaporates without reaching soil water reserves, and much of the water that does soak in is used by the trees themselves [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1].
conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment, with groundwater recharge counted as a component, not whether the restored land itself holds more. Local supply sits in the water stress rows, and a loss here can coexist with a gain there, since the trees use much of the water that soaks in [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1]. The two syntheses read scale differently: in the systematic review the decrease shrinks at larger temporal and spatial scales [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3], while the global review failed to detect a statistically significant relationship in small watersheds and found the reduction significant only in large ones [ev_water_yield_zhang17_2, ev_water_yield_zhang17_3]. The same global review records about 19 small watersheds and a large watershed with increased annual runoff due to forest cover gain, a minority reversal of the usual direction [ev_water_yield_zhang17_5]. Both reviews pool restoration with other forms of forest cover gain; the systematic review reports vote counts rather than pooled sizes, is dominated by temperate and Oceania studies, and the baseflow cases are few [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_2]. One further unit is carried but does not vote: by 25 to 35 years after forest harvest in temperate basins, summer streamflow declined by up to 30%–50% relative to the reference basins [ev_water_yield_jon12_1]. Its comparator is intact old forest, not unrestored land similar to the starting point before regrowth, so it measures how far regenerating forest falls short of the reference rather than what restoration changes; it is a recovery shortfall and is kept out of the class.

effect_mechanism: In Ethiopia, catchments under exclosure pass more baseflow downstream than cropland does: baseflow from catchments with exclosures was 1.5 to 4 times greater than the baseflow from cropland [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1]. At long-term research sites in the USA, forest succession and declining evapotranspiration may explain increased summer streamflow at two temperate forest sites logged in the early nineteenth century [ev_water_yield_jon12_3]. Against these, an FAO synthesis reports that after forest clearance the streamflow gain declines, irregularly, as the new cover establishes, and that a return to pre-cut streamflow totals in the case of natural regrowth may take more than eight years [ev_water_yield_ham08_8].
conditionality: What separates the sides is the starting point and the time scale. The FAO unit is about regrowth on freshly cleared land, where the gain in streamflow from cutting is used up again as the new cover grows [ev_water_yield_ham08_8]; it is harvest-recovery evidence, not a comparison with long-degraded land. The gains compare exclosures with cropland rather than with unrestored land, so that size is a contrast with farmed land, not a measured restoration gain [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1], and the US result is a tentative attribution at sites logged long ago, with no intervention described [ev_water_yield_jon12_3]. The positive class runs against the measured syntheses on forest cover expansion in the other catchment water yield rows; whether regeneration behaves differently from planting in this respect is suggested here, not shown. This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment, not whether the restored land itself holds more.

effect_mechanism: Afforesting grasslands and shrublands reduced annual runoff on average by 44% and 31%, with proportionally larger reductions for low flow and losses of 62% at the driest grassland site [ev_water_yield_farley05_1, ev_water_yield_farley05_2, ev_water_yield_farley05_3, ev_water_yield_farley05_4]. Cases in an FAO synthesis agree: the Fiji Pine Commission's planting of Caribbean Pinus in dry-zone grasslands resulted in dry-season streamflow reductions of 65 percent [ev_water_yield_ham08_7], and in South Africa, where nearly all plantations are on previously native grasslands, water reductions are in some cases experienced as soon as two years after planting, with maximum streamflow decreases relatively early in fast-growing stands [ev_water_yield_ham08_10]. A review of nature-based solutions reports that China's Grain-for-Green programme succeeded in rapidly increasing tree cover but used mainly fast-growing non-native species that have reduced water supply [ev_water_yield_seddon21_10], and adds that single-aged, low diversity, intensively managed plantations may reduce water availability in arid regions [ev_water_yield_seddon21_9]. A national-scale model for New Zealand finds new radiata pine forests on pasture and tussock reduce water yield by between 30% and 50%, through increased interception of rainfall and evaporation by the forest canopy [ev_water_yield_dymond12_2].
conditionality: These are afforestation and plantation-forestry results, mostly from paired catchments and from grassland replaced by fast-growing exotic stands; the authors suggest the effects on water yield will be more severe in drier regions [ev_water_yield_farley05_4], and in South Africa the maximum decreases occur early and then diminish [ev_water_yield_ham08_10]. Forest plantations of native tree species aged 25 to 45 years produce persistent dry-season streamflow deficits exceeding 50% relative to native old-growth forests, because of high water use by young, densely-spaced trees [ev_water_regulation_iufro18_3]; that comparison is against old-growth forest rather than the land the plantation replaced, so it is held out of the class as a reference shortfall. The New Zealand figure is modelled, and its authors note the loss can neutralise the erosion and carbon benefits of new forest in catchments where there is demand for irrigation water [ev_water_yield_dymond12_2]. The Grain-for-Green result is a review sentence carrying cited findings, re-homed here from the restoration families because it describes planting of mainly fast-growing non-native species. The plantation family is parked out of the forest-restoration roll-up and this row is published on its own: read it as evidence about plantations, not about restoration toward a natural baseline.

effect_mechanism: Forests use more water than the land cover that replaces them, so standing forest passes less water downstream: as both natural and human-established forests use more water than most replacement land cover, even partial forest removal increases downstream water yields [ev_water_yield_ham08_1], and replacing forest cover with other land uses almost always results in increased runoff and streamflow [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_2]. All of almost 100 paired catchment experiments involving removal of forest cover gave higher streamflow totals [ev_water_yield_ham08_4]; first-year increases after clearance in the humid tropics range from 110 to 825 mm depending on local rainfall [ev_water_yield_ham08_3], the greatest percentage increase falls in the dry season [ev_water_yield_ham08_2], and daily late-summer flows rose by up to 300% after experimental harvest, though most daily changes were 50% or less [ev_water_yield_jon12_2]. Global syntheses agree: more forest cover loss tends to increase annual runoff in both large and small watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_1], an increase in forest coverage reduces the share of rainfall leaving as runoff [ev_water_yield_zhou15_1], and changes to forests in water-limited watersheds can lead to larger water-yield responses [ev_water_yield_zhou15_2]. Harvesting or removing forest also raises groundwater levels [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_1].
conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment, not whether the restored land itself holds more, and it can coexist with the local gains recorded in the protection water stress row. Every unit compares existing forest with its harvest, clearance or loss, which is why the row sits in the protection family and not in the forest restoration roll-up; none measures the outcome of a protection or community forest management project. One measured result runs the other way: very small summer events decreased by more than 40% in the first 2 years after canopy removal in the Fox Creek basins [ev_water_yield_jon00_1]. The comparison of regenerating basins against uncut reference forest has left this row; it is carried in the cross-family row as a recovery shortfall that does not vote. The null stays named: 12 (of 61) large and 33 (of 252) small watersheds showed no significant change in annual runoff despite forest cover loss [ev_water_yield_zhang17_4]. The groundwater statement also cuts both ways: planting forests on open land where the water table is close to the surface will lower groundwater levels, improving drainage, while removal can move soil salts into the rooting zone [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_1].

justification.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state an effect: a single compiler rating from Niger, with no measured drought outcome [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_2325_2017_drought_impacts]. An FAO review states it is well established that partial or complete removal of tree cover accelerates water discharge, increasing the risk of drought in the dry season [ev_drought_hazard_ham08_1].
conditionality: The strong class rests on thin ground: a single compiler rating, not a measured drought outcome, and a review statement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_drought_impacts]. The FAO statement is about what existing forest does and what its removal costs, not the result of a protection or restoration project, which is why it counts in the protection family only [ev_drought_hazard_ham08_1]. The same review reports elsewhere that removal raises dry-season streamflow (see the protection catchment water yield row), so the dry-season direction is not settled within that source. Read the class as a direction to check locally rather than a measured size.

effect_mechanism: Reforestation slows storm runoff and lowers flood peaks in catchment models: in Slovakia's Hornad watershed a 50% increase of forest cut a simulated flood peak from 84.8 to 74.9 m3/s and reduced peaks by about 24% on average in rain-duration tests, more for short storms than long ones [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_1, ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_3], and an afforestation simulation for Luxembourg's Alzette basin decreased the peak by 8% [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_5]. A systematic review of forest cover and catchment flooding finds peak flow changes by roughly half the change in forest cover, so a 20% increase in forest cover tends to reduce peak flow by 10% across small, medium and large catchments, with only minor differences in mean reductions across event intensities up to the 1% AEP event; it attributes this to forests detaining floodwater through infiltration, canopy interception and evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_1, ev_flood_hazard_herath25_5]. Another systematic review found that flooding or peak flows decreased with forest cover expansion in 82% of studies reporting them [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. In a US experimental basin the gradual recovery of peak discharges over time after clear-cutting, as vegetation regrew, is attributed to changes in evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. An FAO synthesis accepts that locally, for frequent short, low-intensity storm events, flash flooding should be reduced where soils are deep [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_7], and a cited synthesis expects afforestation in energy-limited environments to help reduce flood risks [ev_flood_hazard_zhang17_1]. An Ethiopian WOCAT compiler for a regeneration-based technology rates downstream flooding as strongly reduced, noting that runoff from the watershed is highly reduced [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1072_2011_downstream_flooding].
conditionality: The benefit is off-site for farmers: it lands on downstream flood exposure, not on the restored plot. It is also scale- and storm-bound. The same FAO synthesis that accepts the local effect calls it a misperception that reforesting watersheds reduces or prevents floods, with no evidence for this except at the very local scale of a few hundred hectares [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_5, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_6]. Himalayan position papers reach the same null: estimated peak rainfall intensities balanced against soil infiltration capacities lead to the conclusion that reforestation will not likely have significant beneficial impact on local flooding, and certainly not on the Ganges and Brahmaputra mainstreams [ev_flood_hazard_ives87_1], and reforestation in the mountains conceived as a palliative for the plains is likely to reap only disappointment [ev_flood_hazard_ivesmt87_1]. An FAO–CIFOR review concludes that massive programmes of forestation proclaimed as the answer to preventing floods simply will not do the job, although reforestation may have many other benefits [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_3], and a comment on a global flood analysis argues that reforestation does not necessarily reduce flooding, for example if soil properties do not recover, river bed morphology does not change, and settlements, roads and drains remain unaltered [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_5]. These nulls are expert positions rather than measurements. The flood-cover review adds that afforestation yields only gradual reductions, smaller than the rises in peak flow that follow deforestation and shaped by forest maturity, with peak flow in small catchments falling by up to 14% on limited data; its pooled peak-flow points, including those up to the 1% AEP event, come from other studies' modelled scenarios in mostly temperate catchments [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_2, ev_flood_hazard_herath25_4, ev_flood_hazard_herath25_5]. The modelled benefit shrinks as rain continues, from 29% for the shortest rain duration to 17% for the longest [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_3], and all catchment results are scenarios of large forest-cover gains in temperate high-income basins; the largest figure, a 42.3% peak reduction from converting all arable land to forest, is a secondary citation with no basin named [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_4]. The US regrowth result describes a basin recovering from clear-cutting, not a restoration project [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. The forest-water review pools restoration with forestry and afforestation and reports vote counts rather than magnitudes [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1], and the low- and middle-income evidence consists of a WOCAT compiler rating and expert positions, not measured flows or flood damage. Studies of what existing forest does, such as harvest experiments, sit in the protection family row and do not count here.

effect_mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings the strong reduction rests on a single practitioner judgement: an Ethiopian WOCAT compiler for area closure on degraded land rates downstream flooding as strongly reduced, noting that runoff from the watershed is highly reduced [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1072_2011_downstream_flooding].
conditionality: The strong class stands on a lone compiler rating, not a measured change in flood peaks or damage, and the Himalayan evidence pulls the other way [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1072_2011_downstream_flooding]. Ives, citing the infiltration analysis of Gilmour and colleagues in Nepal's Middle Mountains, concludes that estimated peak rainfall intensities balanced against soil infiltration capacities mean reforestation will not likely have significant beneficial impact on local flooding, and certainly not on the Ganges and Brahmaputra mainstreams [ev_flood_hazard_ives87_1]; the Himalayan conference conclusions warn that reforestation in the mountains conceived as a palliative for the problems of the plains is likely to reap only disappointment [ev_flood_hazard_ivesmt87_1]. What separates the sides is scale: the Ethiopian rating speaks to runoff from a small closed watershed, while the Himalayan nulls address large-river floods and steep slopes where intense rain exceeds what soils can absorb. The Himalayan nulls are expert positions sharing a lead author, and the conference states the mountain-plains link is unproven rather than proven false, so they mark an evidence gap rather than a demonstrated zero [ev_flood_hazard_ivesmt87_1]. Treat this row as a weak lead for small catchments, not as a flood defence for river plains.

effect_mechanism: Both units in this row argue that planting trees does not by itself reduce floods. effect_mechanism: This row describes the flood regulation that standing forest provides and that protection keeps. It is well established that partial or complete removal of tree cover accelerates water discharge, increasing the risk of flood during the rainy season [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_1], and for frequent rainfall events of short duration or low intensity, forested soils may reduce or prevent flash floods locally [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_3]; forests and forest soils reduce runoff through enhanced infiltration and storage, and peak flows rise after forest removal in small experimental catchments [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_1, ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_2]. Paired-basin experiments in high-income Oregon, USA, measure the cost of harvest: forest harvesting increased peak discharges by as much as 50% in small basins and 100% in large basins over 50 years, attributable to roads and to water-balance changes [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_1]; in small basins discharges rose by 50% in the first 5 years and stayed 25 to 40% above pretreatment up to 25 years later [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_2, ev_flood_hazard_jg96_3]; and in 100%-clear-cut basins large events increased by 25%, 16% and 26% at Andrews 1, Andrews 6 and Coyote 3 [ev_flood_hazard_jon00_1]. The same Oregon study separates the event types. Forest canopy removal accounted for significant increases (31–116%) in peak discharges during the first postharvest decade in 8 of 10 treated basins, but the affected events were small and fell in the fall (September–November), when soils are in moisture deficit, rather than in spring [ev_water_regulation_jon00_1]. Changes in snowpack dynamics accounted for significant increases (25–31%) in winter rain-on-snow events in four of five basins at the H. J. Andrews Experimental Forest [ev_water_regulation_jon00_6]. A country-level analysis of developing countries predicted that a further hypothetical 10% loss of natural forest cover would raise flood frequency by 3.5% to 28.1% and flood duration by 3.8% to 7.9% [ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_1, ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_2]; in Peninsular Malaysia, a river-basin panel study by Tan-Soo and colleagues found that converting 1% of a basin from inland forest to oil palm increased the number of days flooded by 26.8%, and to rubber by 26.5%, with conversion to urban use also having a large effect (semi-elasticity = 35.9%) [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_1, ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_2, ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_4]; a systematic review of forest cover and catchment flooding finds that deforestation consistently increases peak flows [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_3]; and in Swiss valleys with more than 30% forest snowmelt was more gradual and flooding risk lower [ev_flood_hazard_iufro18_2].
conditionality: The class is moderate because the evidence agrees only in part: the service fades with storm size and basin size. For the rarer prolonged or high-intensity storms, once the soil layer becomes saturated, water runs off even under full, undisturbed forest cover [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_4]; forest soils reduce runoff only in small-scale rainfall events, which are not responsible for severe downstream flooding, and forests cannot stop catastrophic large-scale floods caused by severe meteorological events [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_1, ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_2]; small to medium peak flows are affected most while the largest events do not change noticeably, and studies in larger basins have not usually found changes after deforestation of up to 50% of the catchment [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_3, ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_4]. The harvest experiments carry their own nulls: complete clear-cutting without roads raised fall and winter events but not large events as a group [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_4], large events did not change at Andrews 10 [ev_flood_hazard_jon00_2], other types of winter events did not change beside rain-on-snow events [ev_water_regulation_jon00_7], cloud water interception apparently offset evapotranspiration changes in two partially cut, fog-prone basins [ev_water_regulation_jon00_5], the fall increases were confined to small events [ev_water_regulation_jon00_1], and the large-basin increases are bundled with forest road construction, so they cannot be credited to forest cover alone [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_1]. The Malaysian study also carries the harm finding in this row: where the forest converted was wetland (peat-swamp) forest, deforestation reduced flooding, a large effect (semi-elasticity = 38.0%), which the authors link to drainage installed at conversion lowering the water level; so keeping forest is not a flood defence in every forest type [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_3]. The same study found no significant effect of deforestation on the number of floods per month, which the authors put down to a problem in defining that variable [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_5]; its inland-forest figures are semi-elasticities per 1% of basin area converted, not whole-catchment contrasts, and the urban figure was not estimated very precisely (P = 0.094) [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_4]. A worldwide review found no cause and effect demonstrated between forest cutting in the headwaters and floods in the lower basin, with no conflicting information published more than 20 years later [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_2], and on the Himalayan scale human influences on plains flooding are contended to be insignificant so far [ev_flood_hazard_ives87_2]. The cross-country analysis itself found little evidence that further forest loss changed flood deaths or damage [ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_3, ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_4], and a reanalysis of its data found the correlation between forest cover or cover loss and flood frequency appears absent, with the degraded-lands fraction accounting for most of the variation [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_1]. Every unit compares forest with cleared or less-forested land, so the row shows what losing forest costs rather than the outcome of a protection or community forestry programme; that is why these units sit in the protection family and not in the restoration roll-up. Benefits fall downstream, off-site for farmers.

effect_mechanism: Restoration and co-managed forest improve food security mainly through more fodder, water and forest foods around regenerating sites, though the measured gain is small. In Niger the compiler for assisted natural regeneration on agro-pastoral, sylvo-pastoral and pastoral land reports that it contributes to food security and food self-sufficiency in the southern regions, estimates the impact at 20% at least, and notes that in the northern pastoral zone it reduces forage deficits so that livestock keepers are not forced to sell their animals in the lean season [ev_food_security_wocat_2325_2017_food_security_selfsufficiency]. In India the compiler for broadleaf plantations, assisted tree regeneration and fodder nurseries reports better village self-sufficiency because animal productivity rose with more and better fodder and water availability increased [ev_food_security_wocat_5243_2019_food_security_selfsufficiency]. In Malawi, households taking part in forest co-management through village natural resource management committees had a 1.62% higher food consumption score than non-participants, with wild foods collected from the reserves as the pathway the authors describe [ev_food_security_kimwanga26_3].
conditionality: The slight class is set by the measured Malawi survey: the food consumption gain from co-management is small, and it pulls the row down from the strong Niger and India compiler ratings, which are judgements rather than measured changes in hunger or food consumption [ev_food_security_kimwanga26_3, ev_food_security_wocat_2325_2017_food_security_selfsufficiency, ev_food_security_wocat_5243_2019_food_security_selfsufficiency]. Food security does not always rise. The Cabo Verde afforestation compiler rates food self-sufficiency unchanged because the practice reduces the options of land use [ev_food_security_wocat_1523_2011_food_security_selfsufficiency], and under Mexico's payments for environmental services, as cited in a systematic review, households in common-property areas showed a statistically insignificant food-index effect of 0.09 SMD [ev_food_security_snilstveit19_1]; that unit concerns a payment scheme rather than a restoration practice. The Malawi result is a cross-sectional comparison of committee members with non-members, not a before-and-after measure. Studies of what existing forest and protected areas provide for diets are kept to the protection and community forest management row and do not count here.

effect_mechanism: Where restoration narrows the production gap, it does so through cropland downstream of or next to restored land, and through fodder; on the restored land itself, soil nitrogen can fall. In Tigray, Ethiopia, households downstream of exclosures harvested 188 to 222 kg/ha more than those beside open grazing areas in the drought-affected 2023 season, and a panel estimate put the grain advantage at 586.6 kg/ha [ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_1, ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_2]. In Brazil the Reflorestar payments-for-ecosystem-services programme raised agricultural value added by 8% and the value of agricultural production by approximately 14% in the poorest quarter of municipalities [ev_agricultural_production_value_seixas24_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_seixas24_3]. WOCAT compilers give the on-farm pathways: an Ethiopian area closure raised crop production because soil depth increased and soil fertility improved, Tanzanian enclosures raised crop production through mulching materials, fodder through area enclosure and decline of forest fire, and animal production through nutritious cut and carry pastures, and in Turkmenistan the planted sand fixing species are also used as forage [ev_crop_yield_wocat_1072_2011_crop_production, ev_crop_yield_wocat_1607_2014_crop_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_1607_2014_fodder_production, ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_1607_2014_animal_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_1529_2012_fodder_production]. On the other side, a meta-analysis of vegetation restoration in erosion zones found that returning cropland or bare land to forest left soil total nitrogen content not significantly changed overall (3.04%), and that it decreased by 16.84% in hot regions (MAT > 15 °C) and by 19.85% in humid regions (MAP > 800 mm) compared with cropland; the authors attribute this to higher plant uptake of soil nitrogen under high temperature and rainfall [ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_4, ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_6, ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_7].
conditionality: The sub-practice rows disagree, so no direction is stated. The passive regeneration row reads a strong gain from the Tigray exclosure yields [ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_1, ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_2], while the cross-family row is itself conflicted, with the Brazilian programme gains set against the soil nitrogen losses [ev_agricultural_production_value_seixas24_3, ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_6, ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_7]. What separates them is where production is measured and the climate: the gains are crop, fodder or production-value results on farmland beside or downstream of restored land, while the nitrogen losses describe the soil of land converted from cropland to forest in hot or humid regions, which is the measured harm on this row [ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_6, ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_7]. justification.mechanism: In these upper-middle-income settings the evidence points both ways. On the gain side, farm output rose alongside restoration: under Brazil's Reflorestar payments programme, agricultural value added in the poorest-quartile municipalities rose by 8% and the value of agricultural production by approximately 14% [ev_agricultural_production_value_seixas24_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_seixas24_3], and on Turkmen barkhan sands the compiler rates fodder production as strongly increased because the planted sand-fixing species are also used as forage [ev_forage_productivity_wocat_1529_2012_fodder_production]. On the loss side, a meta-analysis of vegetation restoration in erosion zones found that returning cropland or bare land to forest left soil total nitrogen content not significantly changed overall (3.04%), and that it decreased by 16.84% in hot regions (MAT > 15 °C) and by 19.85% in humid regions (MAP > 800 mm) compared with cropland; the authors attribute this to higher plant uptake of soil nitrogen under high temperature and rainfall [ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_4, ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_6, ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_7].
justification.conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates them is what is measured and where. The gains are production value and forage on farmland and planted dunes [ev_agricultural_production_value_seixas24_3, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_1529_2012_fodder_production]; the losses are soil nitrogen on land converted from cropland to forest, confined to hot and humid regions, with no significant change across all sites [ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_4, ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_6, ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_7]. The nitrogen units are a component of the production gap rather than a yield measurement, the meta-analysis does not report where its studies were, and its subgroup significance is shown only in a figure. The Brazilian result is a municipal-scale programme effect confined to the poorest-quartile municipalities and measured as production value rather than yield; it reflects a payment programme rather than a restoration practice alone, so the route from trees to farm output is not shown [ev_agricultural_production_value_seixas24_2]. The Turkmen unit is a practitioner rating, and its gain is forage from the planted shrubs, a component of the production gap rather than crop yield [ev_forage_productivity_wocat_1529_2012_fodder_production].

effect_mechanism: Enclosing degraded land lets vegetation and soil recover, and the gain reaches production through fodder and nearby cropland. In Tanzania the compiler for an enclosure rates fodder production as increased because of area enclosure and the decline of forest fire, animal production as increased through nutritious cut and carry pastures, and crop production as increased through mulching materials used by some farmers [ev_forage_productivity_wocat_1607_2014_fodder_production, ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_1607_2014_animal_production, ev_crop_yield_wocat_1607_2014_crop_production]. An Ethiopian compiler rates crop production as strongly increased because soil depth increased and soil fertility improved [ev_crop_yield_wocat_1072_2011_crop_production]. In Tigray, Ethiopia, households downstream of exclosures harvested 188 to 222 kg/ha more than those beside open grazing areas in the drought-affected 2023 season, and a panel estimate put the grain advantage at 586.6 kg/ha [ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_1, ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_2].
conditionality: The measured advantage is concentrated in the drier year: the exclosure benefit was greater in the first, drier year (an interaction of −298 kg/ha), and no statistically significant yield difference was found in the second production year (2024/2025) [ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_3, ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_4]. It concerns downstream cropland compared with open grazing, not the enclosed land itself. The other units are practitioner ratings, not measurements, and much of their gain runs through fodder and livestock, a component of the production gap rather than crop yield.
